decisions.quote: This study replicates the findings from Braxton et al. (Res High Educ 39(3):299–318, 1998) using student-level rather than faculty-level reports of faculty use of good teaching practices.
decisions.reason: In the supplied abstract, the authors first state their purpose and methods in the opening two sentences, then report their empirical results across the six principles in the next two sentences, and conclude the abstract with the final sentence: 'This study replicates the findings from Braxton et al. (Res High Educ 39(3):299–318, 1998) using student-level rather than faculty-level reports of faculty use of good teaching practices.' Placed at the end of the abstract after the results and taking 'the findings from Braxton et al.' as its direct object, this sentence is an explicit overall author verdict under Rule 1 that the original findings were replicated, making the outcome 'successful' without requiring an item-by-item enumeration of the original study's results.

scope_review.parent_objection: The abstract ends, after detailed Results, with This study replicates the findings from Braxton et al. (1998) using student-level rather than faculty-level reports. Is that a genuine overall verdict that replication findings match, under Rule1, or merely design/intent language? First reply withholds because original-specific results not enumerated and present-tense replicates could be design. Rule1 does not require enumerating original findings when authors give a genuine overall verdict. Do not infer mixed merely because this paper has both significant and null results across measures. Read complete supplied abstract and context; decide semantic scope of actual ending, with direct quotation. Unseen full text cannot automatically veto an explicit available verdict.

prior_reply.quote: Our findings suggest that as paradigmatic development increases (toward a higher proportion of courses taken in hard disciplines), student perceptions of both faculty use of prompt feedback and faculty use of high expectations/academic challenge decrease, while student perceptions of cooperative learning increase. Further, no statistically significant differences were found between the paradigmatic development of fields in which students’ take their courses and students’ perceptions of faculty use of student-faculty contact, active and collaborative learning, or teaching clarity and organization. This study replicates the findings from Braxton et al. (Res High Educ 39(3):299–318, 1998) using student-level rather than faculty-level reports of faculty use of good teaching practices.
prior_reply.reason: Only the abstract is available, which reports mixed directional and null effects across the six principles without stating what Braxton et al. (1998) originally found on each principle, and its final sentence is ambiguous between stating the replication design and claiming an overall confirmation. Without the unseen full text comparing the specific findings to Braxton et al. (1998), the outcome cannot be definitively adjudicated between mixed and successful.
